questions.question: Which of the following scientists is credited with the mathematical unification of electricity and magnetism?
questions.answer: Maxwell's equations described electric and magnetic fields in one mathematical framework, unifying electricity and magnetism (and predicting electromagnetic waves).

questions.question: Which of the following is a standard assumption when analysing the motion of projectiles?
options: The path of the projectile is an ellipse
questions.answer: The standard projectile model assumes zero air resistance and a constant (uniform) vertical acceleration $g$ downwards, giving a parabolic path.

questions.question: The force of gravity between two objects is $F$. What happens to the force of gravity between both objects if the distance between the objects is doubled?
questions.answer: $F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$, an inverse-square law. Doubling $r$ gives $\dfrac{F}{2^2} = \dfrac{F}{4}$.

questions.question: Which of the following variables need to be aligned for a satellite to be in geostationary orbit around a planet?
options: The orbital velocity of both the satellite and the planet are equal.
The period of one revolution of the satellite is equal to the time taken for one spin of the planet on its axis.
The period of the planet and the satellite is equal.
The mass of the planet and the satellite must be equal.
questions.answer: A geostationary satellite stays above the same point on the surface, so its orbital period must equal the planet's rotational period (24 h for Earth), orbiting in the same direction above the equator.

questions.question: A person with a viral infection has their body temperature rise from 37 °C (310 K) to 40 °C. What is the change in the peak wavelength of electromagnetic radiation emitted?
questions.answer: Wien's law $\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{b}{T}$: $\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{310} = 9.348\times10^{-6}$ m and $\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{313} = 9.259\times10^{-6}$ m. The peak wavelength decreases by $8.96\times10^{-8}$ m (higher temperature → shorter peak wavelength).

questions.question:
An 0.800 kg mass is swinging in a horizontal circle on the end of a conical pendulum as shown. The radius of the circle $r$ is 0.25 m and the period $T$ is 2.0 s.

What is the kinetic energy of the mass?
questions.answer: $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi(0.25)}{2.0} = 0.785\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so $K = \tfrac12 mv^2 = \tfrac12(0.800)(0.785)^2 = 0.25$ J. (Note: options B and D in the original paper are identical, and both were accepted; 0.79 is the speed, not the energy.)

questions.question:
Several planets with identical size but different masses had their surface gravitational acceleration, $g$, plotted against their masses, $M$.

Which alternative best represents this graph?
questions.answer: $g = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$. With $r$ the same for every planet, $g \propto M$: a straight line through the origin.

questions.question: How does back EMF affect the operation of an electric motor?
options: It prevents the motor from starting.
It increases the power output of the motor.
It increases the current drawn from the power source.
It reduces the current drawn from the power source when the motor speeds up.
questions.answer: As the coil rotates faster, the induced back emf (which opposes the supply emf, by Lenz's law) increases, so the net emf and hence the current drawn from the supply decrease.

questions.question:
The following graph plots data for a number of galaxies.

Which of the following is true about the trend shown in this graph?
options: It is linear because all galaxies are receding at the same rate.
It provides evidence for the 'Big Bang'.
It shows that the expansion of the universe is slowing.
It proves that every galaxy is redshifted.
questions.answer: The graph shows Hubble's law: recession velocity is proportional to distance, so more distant galaxies recede faster. This expansion of the universe is evidence for the Big Bang. (Galaxies recede at different rates; one data set cannot show slowing or *prove* every galaxy is redshifted.)

questions.question: The role of a commutator in a DC motor is to:
options: change the direction of current relative to the coil.
keep the current flowing in the same direction relative to the coil.
questions.answer: The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so the torque on the coil keeps acting in the same rotational direction.

questions.question: Calculate the wavelength of a tennis ball of mass 59.4 g travelling at 170 km h$^{-1}$.
In each diagram below, a rectangular coil connected to a split-ring commutator sits in a magnetic field (dotted arrows). Which of the following scenarios will produce the greatest torque on the coil?
questions.answer: $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$. In B the plane of the coil is parallel to the field (maximum torque) and the coil has two turns, so $n$ is largest. In C the field is perpendicular to the plane of the coil, giving zero torque.

questions.question: Which of the following is an observation from the Hafele–Keating experiment that supports Einstein's theory of special relativity?
options: Clocks flown westward (in the opposite direction to Earth's rotation) were slowed the most.
Clocks flown eastward (in the same direction as Earth's rotation) were slowed the most.
Clocks flown eastward and westward were equally slowed.
Clocks flown eastward and westward were not slowed.
questions.answer: Relative to an inertial frame at Earth's centre, eastward-flying clocks move fastest (plane speed adds to Earth's rotation), so they experienced the most time dilation and lost time relative to ground clocks; westward clocks moved slowest and gained time.

questions.question: A Ferris wheel car covers an arc distance of 62.8 metres in 2 minutes. If the radius of the Ferris wheel is 10 metres, what is the angular velocity in degrees per second?
questions.answer: $\theta = \dfrac{s}{r} = \dfrac{62.8}{10} = 6.28$ rad $= 360^\circ$, in 120 s. $\omega = \dfrac{360^\circ}{120\ \text{s}} = 3.00^\circ\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.question:
The apparatus shown below was set up to measure the force between two parallel current-carrying conductors 1.5 cm apart, each carrying a current of 12 A. Before the current was turned on, the scale was zeroed; with the current on, the scale reads 0.042 g.

Determine the length $L$ of the two current-carrying conductors shown in the image above.

A car of mass 1200 kg is driving in a horizontal circular track of radius 50 metres with a constant speed of 20 m s$^{-1}$. If the coefficient of friction between the car's tyres and the track is 0.1, what is the work done by friction over one complete revolution?
questions.answer: Friction provides the centripetal force, which always acts towards the centre, perpendicular to the velocity. A force perpendicular to the displacement does no work ($W = Fs\cos 90^\circ = 0$); consistent with this, the speed and kinetic energy are constant.

questions.question: If the value of Planck's constant, $h$, was higher than it is, the effect on a photoelectric effect experiment would be:
options: the photoelectric current would be greater.
the energy of incident photons would be less.
the threshold frequency would be greater for all metals.
the threshold frequency would be lower for all metals.
questions.answer: Threshold frequency $f_0 = \dfrac{\phi}{h}$. For the same work function, a larger $h$ gives a smaller $f_0$ for every metal. (Photon energy $hf$ would be larger, not smaller.)

questions.question: How long does it take to emit one million photons from a 10 mW laser with frequency $4.5 \times 10^{14}$ Hz?

A ring of area $A$ is hung by a fishing line so that it sits within a uniform magnetic field $B$ directed into the page, as shown below (the plane of the ring is perpendicular to the field).

Determine the change in flux when the ring spins from its position by $120^\circ$.
questions.answer: $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$. Initially $\theta = 0$: $\Phi_i = BA$. After $120^\circ$: $\Phi_f = BA\cos120^\circ = -\tfrac12 BA$. $\Delta\Phi = -\tfrac12 BA - BA = -\tfrac32 BA$.

questions.question:
The following experimental set-up can be used to produce a 'Poisson Spot': a bright spot that can be seen in the centre of a circular object's shadow.

Which of the following would increase the size of the Poisson Spot?
options: Moving the light source closer to the circular object
Moving the circular object closer to the screen
Increasing the wavelength of the light source
Increasing the diameter of the circular object
questions.answer: The Poisson spot is produced by diffraction of light around the edge of the object and constructive interference at the centre of the shadow. The amount of diffraction (and so the size of the spot) increases with wavelength.

questions.question: A current-carrying conductor of length 1.5 m is placed in a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.5 T. Determine the magnitude of the magnetic force experienced by the current-carrying conductor if the current through the conductor is 0.6 A and the current flows perpendicular to the magnetic field.
questions.answer: $F = lIB\sin\theta = 1.5 \times 0.6 \times 0.5 \times \sin 90^\circ = 0.45$ N

questions.question: Describe how spectra provide information about TWO features of stars.
questions.answer:
Stellar spectra are absorption spectra: a continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines where gases in the star's outer layers absorb particular wavelengths.

- **Chemical composition:** each element absorbs at its own characteristic set of wavelengths, so matching the dark lines in a star's spectrum with laboratory spectra of elements identifies the elements present in the star's atmosphere.
- **Translational (radial) velocity:** if the absorption lines are shifted towards longer wavelengths (lower frequency, red shift) compared with laboratory values, the star is moving away from the observer; a blue shift means it is approaching. The size of the shift gives the speed.

Other acceptable features: surface temperature (peak wavelength of the continuous spectrum, Wien's law, and which lines are present); density (broad, wide lines indicate dense stars with high-pressure atmospheres, narrow lines less dense giants); rotational velocity (light from one edge is red-shifted and the other blue-shifted, broadening the lines).

questions.question:
Following a lesson on Special Relativity, a student made the following statement:

> “The surface of the Earth is not an inertial frame of reference”

Assess the validity of this statement.
questions.answer:
An inertial frame of reference is one that is not accelerating (moving at constant velocity), in which Newton's first law holds. A point on the surface of the Earth moves in a circle as the Earth rotates on its axis, and the Earth also orbits the Sun, so the surface is continually changing direction — it has a centripetal acceleration. Therefore the surface of the Earth is strictly a non-inertial frame, and the statement is valid.

(For many everyday experiments these accelerations are very small, so the Earth's surface is often *approximated* as an inertial frame — but strictly the statement is correct.)

questions.question:
On 4 May 1989, the objective of the Magellan mission to Venus was to place a satellite in orbit to image the entire surface of the planet.

Mass of Venus $= 4.867 \times 10^{24}$ kg; mass of satellite $= 3445$ kg; orbital radius $= 6.346 \times 10^{6}$ m.

Determine the orbital period of the satellite around Venus. Assume a circular orbit.
questions.answer:
$$\frac{r^3}{T^2} = \frac{GM}{4\pi^2} \Rightarrow T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 r^3}{GM} = \frac{4\pi^2(6.346\times10^{6})^3}{6.67\times10^{-11}\times4.867\times10^{24}} = 3.108\times10^{7}$$

$T = 5.57\times10^{3}$ s (about 92.9 minutes).

questions.question:
On 4 May 1989, the objective of the Magellan mission to Venus was to place a satellite in orbit to image the entire surface of the planet.

Mass of Venus $= 4.867 \times 10^{24}$ kg; mass of satellite $= 3445$ kg; orbital radius $= 6.346 \times 10^{6}$ m.

How much additional work would need to be done for the satellite to escape the planet, Venus? Use relevant equations and calculations to support your answer.
questions.answer:
For a satellite to escape to infinity its total mechanical energy must be raised to (at least) zero.

In a circular orbit, $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ and $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, so the total energy is

$$E = U + K = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = -\frac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times4.867\times10^{24}\times3445}{2\times6.346\times10^{6}} = -8.81\times10^{10}\ \text{J}$$

The additional work required (e.g. by rocket boosters) is $8.81\times10^{10}$ J, increasing the total energy from $-8.81\times10^{10}$ J to zero.

(Note: the paper's sample answer writes $8.81\times10^{13}$ J in its final sentence; its own working gives $8.81\times10^{10}$ J, which is correct.)

questions.question:
A space organisation is planning to send an astronaut to a distant planet, $P$. The spacecraft will travel at a speed of $0.8c$ and the journey is expected to take 15 years, as measured by observers on Earth. The spacecraft and astronaut have a combined mass of 1500 kg.

Calculate the distance to $P$, as measured by observers on Earth.
questions.answer:
$d = vt = 0.8c \times 15\ \text{years} = 12$ light-years.

$d = 0.8 \times 3\times10^{8} \times (15 \times 365 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60) = 1.14\times10^{17}$ m

questions.question:
A space organisation is planning to send an astronaut to a distant planet, $P$. The spacecraft will travel at a speed of $0.8c$ and the journey is expected to take 15 years, as measured by observers on Earth. The spacecraft and astronaut have a combined mass of 1500 kg.

Determine how many years will have passed on the spaceship's clock when observed by Earth.
questions.answer:
The spaceship's clock records the proper time $t_0$; Earth observers measure the dilated time $t = 15$ years.

$$t = \frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}} \Rightarrow t_0 = t\sqrt{1-0.8^2} = 15\times0.6 = 9\ \text{years}$$

questions.question:
The diagram below shows a simplified power distribution network.

Explain why transformers are used in the distribution of energy.
questions.answer: Transformers change the voltage of the AC supply. The power lost as heat in the transmission lines is $P_{\text{loss}} = I^2R$. At the power station a step-up transformer increases the voltage to a very high value; since the power transmitted $P = VI$ is (ideally) unchanged, the current is reduced by the same factor, so the $I^2R$ energy loss in the long transmission lines is greatly reduced and power can be transmitted efficiently over long distances. At the consumer end a step-down transformer reduces the voltage to a safe, usable level (e.g. 240 V for homes).

questions.question:
Before an experiment to find the half-life of a radioactive isotope, a nuclear scientist switched on her radiation counter in the lab for five 60-second intervals and recorded the following background readings (counts/min): 1123, 1126, 1128, 1127, 1121.

The scientist then placed a sample of radioactive isotope $X$ near the counter and measured the counts per minute every second Monday for 14 weeks. Counting the first week as week 0, her results are shown in the table below.

| Time (weeks) | Total radiation recorded (counts/min) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 11125 |
| 2 | 7725 |
| 4 | 5525 |
| 6 | 4125 |
| 8 | 3125 |
| 10 | 2425 |
| 12 | 2075 |
| 14 | 1625 |

Draw a graph to show the relationship between time and the radiation of $X$.
questions.answer:
First subtract the background count. Mean background $= \dfrac{1123+1126+1128+1127+1121}{5} = 1125$ counts/min.

| Time (weeks) | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corrected count rate (counts/min) | 10000 | 6600 | 4400 | 3000 | 2000 | 1300 | 950 | 500 |

Plot corrected count rate (vertical axis) against time in weeks (horizontal axis), with labelled axes and units and uniform scales, and draw a smooth exponential-decay curve of best fit through the points (not a dot-to-dot line).

questions.question:
Before an experiment to find the half-life of a radioactive isotope, a nuclear scientist switched on her radiation counter in the lab for five 60-second intervals and recorded the following background readings (counts/min): 1123, 1126, 1128, 1127, 1121.

The scientist then placed a sample of radioactive isotope $X$ near the counter and measured the counts per minute every second Monday for 14 weeks. Counting the first week as week 0, her results are shown in the table below.

| Time (weeks) | Total radiation recorded (counts/min) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 11125 |
| 2 | 7725 |
| 4 | 5525 |
| 6 | 4125 |
| 8 | 3125 |
| 10 | 2425 |
| 12 | 2075 |
| 14 | 1625 |

After subtracting the background radiation, the count rates are plotted against time and a curve of best fit drawn. Use the graph to show that the half-life of $X$ is approximately 3.4 weeks.
questions.answer: The corrected initial count rate is $11125 - 1125 = 10000$ counts/min. Half of this is 5000 counts/min. Reading across from 5000 counts/min to the curve of best fit and down to the time axis gives $t \approx 3.4$ weeks (between the week 2 value of 6600 and the week 4 value of 4400). So $t_{1/2} \approx 3.4$ weeks.

questions.question:
Before an experiment to find the half-life of a radioactive isotope, a nuclear scientist switched on her radiation counter in the lab for five 60-second intervals and recorded the following background readings (counts/min): 1123, 1126, 1128, 1127, 1121.

The scientist then placed a sample of radioactive isotope $X$ near the counter and measured the counts per minute every second Monday for 14 weeks. Counting the first week as week 0, her results are shown in the table below.

| Time (weeks) | Total radiation recorded (counts/min) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 11125 |
| 2 | 7725 |
| 4 | 5525 |
| 6 | 4125 |
| 8 | 3125 |
| 10 | 2425 |
| 12 | 2075 |
| 14 | 1625 |

Given that the half-life of $X$ is approximately 3.4 weeks, calculate the decay constant.
questions.answer:
$$\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{3.4} = 0.20\ \text{week}^{-1}$$

(Note: the paper's marking guidelines give $\ln 2/3 = 0.23\ \text{week}^{-1}$, which uses a half-life of 3 weeks; with the 3.4-week half-life the decay constant is $0.20\ \text{week}^{-1}$. Answers consistent with the student's own half-life were accepted.)

questions.question:
A uniform magnetic field of strength 0.5 T is directed into the page. An electron and a proton are both fired simultaneously into the magnetic field at $1 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$: the proton enters from the left moving to the right, and the electron enters from the right moving to the left, as shown. Assume the particles do not interact with each other.

Describe the paths that the particles will follow through the magnetic field. Support your answer with relevant calculations.
questions.answer:
Each particle experiences a magnetic force $F = qvB$ perpendicular to its velocity, so each moves in a circular arc (uniform circular motion) with $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, i.e. $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

Electron: $r = \dfrac{9.109\times10^{-31}\times1\times10^{4}}{1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.5} = 1.1\times10^{-7}$ m

Proton: $r = \dfrac{1.673\times10^{-27}\times1\times10^{4}}{1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.5} = 2.1\times10^{-4}$ m

Direction (right-hand rule): the proton (moving right) is pushed towards the top of the page and curves anticlockwise; the electron (moving left, negative charge) is also pushed towards the top of the page and curves clockwise. Both therefore curve upwards initially, in opposite rotational senses. Because the proton's mass is about 1840 times greater, its circular path has a radius about 1840 times larger than the electron's very tight circle.

questions.question:
Below is a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram with two labelled stars, X and Y. The reaction that produces energy in Star X can be summarised as

$$4\,{}^{1}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + 2\,{}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$$

| Nucleus | Mass (amu) |
|---|---|
| ${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ | 4.002603 |
| ${}^{1}_{1}\text{H}$ | 1.007825 |
| ${}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$ | 0.000549 |

Calculate the energy released from this reaction.
questions.answer:
Mass defect: $\Delta m = 4(1.007825) - 4.002603 - 2(0.000549) = 0.027599$ u

$\Delta m = 0.027599 \times 1.661\times10^{-27} = 4.584\times10^{-29}$ kg

$E = \Delta m c^2 = 4.584\times10^{-29}\times(3\times10^{8})^2 = 4.13\times10^{-12}$ J (about 25.7 MeV, since $0.027599 \times 931.5 = 25.7$ MeV).

(Note: the original paper wrote the emitted particles as ${}^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$; charge conservation requires positrons, ${}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$, as above. The calculation is unchanged.)

questions.question:
Below is a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram with two labelled stars, X and Y. The reaction that produces energy in Star X can be summarised as

$$4\,{}^{1}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + 2\,{}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$$

| Nucleus | Mass (amu) |
|---|---|
| ${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ | 4.002603 |
| ${}^{1}_{1}\text{H}$ | 1.007825 |
| ${}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$ | 0.000549 |

Compare the energy production in Star Y to Star X.
questions.answer:
Similarity: both X and Y lie on the main sequence, so both produce energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores.

Differences: Star Y is a hot, high-mass main sequence star (about 20 000 K, luminosity about $10^{2}$–$10^{3}$ times the Sun), whereas X is a cool, low-mass red dwarf (about 3000 K, luminosity about $10^{-4}$ of the Sun). Y's higher core temperature and pressure mean it fuses hydrogen at a far greater rate (much higher energy output/luminosity), and it produces most of its energy by the CNO cycle, while X produces energy mainly by the proton–proton chain. As a result Y will use up its core hydrogen and leave the main sequence much sooner than X.

questions.question:
A student performed an experiment to investigate the light emitted from discharge tubes containing various gases. The student's observations are shown: hydrogen glows pink, neon glows red and argon glows violet.

Explain why the gases emit different colours inside the discharge tubes.
questions.answer:
A high potential difference between the metal electrodes causes a current to pass through the low-pressure gas. Collisions transfer energy to electrons in the gas atoms, exciting them from the ground state to higher energy levels. When an excited electron returns to a lower energy level, the energy difference is emitted as a photon with $E = hf = E_{\text{upper}} - E_{\text{lower}}$.

Each element has its own unique set of electron energy levels, so the allowed transitions — and therefore the frequencies (wavelengths) of the emitted light — are different for each gas. The combination of emitted wavelengths gives each gas its characteristic colour.

questions.question:
A student performed an experiment to investigate the light emitted from discharge tubes containing various gases. The student's observations are shown: hydrogen glows pink, neon glows red and argon glows violet.

The spectra of light from the discharge tubes are examined through a spectroscope. How will these spectra differ from those produced by an incandescent filament?
questions.answer: The discharge tubes produce emission (line) spectra: a discontinuous spectrum of a few bright coloured lines at specific wavelengths, characteristic of each gas, on a dark background. An incandescent filament is a hot solid that emits a continuous (black body) spectrum containing all visible wavelengths, with no gaps.

questions.question:
A physics student, who is also a model train enthusiast, is combining their two interests to undertake a study in electromagnetic induction. They rig up one of their trains with a strong bar magnet on its load carriage and have its track pass through a solenoid. The solenoid is attached to a galvanometer to measure the induced current.

They notice that the train exits the solenoid tunnel with a lower speed than when it entered and does not begin to accelerate to a normal operating speed for a small distance after exiting.

Explain their observations.
questions.answer:
When the train enters the solenoid, the locomotive itself is not magnetic, so it enters at full speed. As the bar magnet on the carriage approaches and enters the solenoid, the magnetic flux through the coils changes. By Faraday's law ($\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$) an emf is induced, and since the solenoid is part of a closed circuit with the galvanometer, a current flows.

By Lenz's law the induced current flows in a direction such that its magnetic field opposes the change in flux that produced it: the solenoid repels the magnet as it approaches and attracts it back as it leaves. Either way the force opposes the magnet's motion, so kinetic energy of the train is converted into electrical energy (and then heat) in the circuit, and the train slows down — consistent with conservation of energy.

The magnetic field of the magnet extends beyond the end of the solenoid, so the flux through the solenoid is still changing just after the carriage exits. The opposing (attractive) force therefore continues to act for a short distance after exiting, delaying the train's return to its normal operating speed until the magnet is far enough away for the induced current to become negligible.

questions.question:
A model rocket, initially on the ground, was launched at an angle of $20.0^\circ$ from the horizontal. After a 2.50 s motor burn, the model had a velocity of 82.0 m s$^{-1}$ and then followed projectile motion for the remainder of its flight.

Determine the horizontal range of the rocket after landing. Assume its initial trajectory did not change during its motor burn (i.e. it accelerated uniformly from rest in a straight line at $20.0^\circ$ to the horizontal).
questions.answer:
**Motor burn (straight line, uniform acceleration from rest):**

$s = \dfrac{u+v}{2}t = \dfrac{0 + 82.0}{2}\times2.50 = 102.5$ m along the launch line.

$\Delta x_1 = 102.5\cos20^\circ = 96.3$ m, $\quad \Delta y_1 = 102.5\sin20^\circ = 35.1$ m

**Projectile phase** (launched from height 35.1 m):

$u_x = 82.0\cos20^\circ = 77.1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $\quad u_y = 82.0\sin20^\circ = 28.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

Taking up as positive, landing when $\Delta y = -35.1$ m:

$-35.1 = 28.0t - 4.9t^2 \Rightarrow 4.9t^2 - 28.0t - 35.1 = 0$

$t = \dfrac{28.0 + \sqrt{28.0^2 + 4(4.9)(35.1)}}{2(4.9)} = 6.77$ s

$\Delta x_2 = u_x t = 77.1 \times 6.77 = 522$ m

**Total horizontal range:** $96.3 + 522 \approx 619$ m (about 618.5 m; the total flight time is $2.50 + 6.77 = 9.27$ s).

questions.question:
Light of a particular frequency is incident on a calcium metal sheet and photoelectrons are emitted. The metal is in a uniform electric field, perpendicular to the surface of the metal, as shown (the field opposes the motion of the electron away from the sheet).

Explain the behaviour of this photoelectron with reference to the law of conservation of energy.
questions.answer:
Each photon gives all its energy $hf$ to one electron. A photoelectron is emitted only if the photon energy exceeds the work function $\phi$ of calcium. By conservation of energy, the remaining energy becomes the electron's kinetic energy: $K_{\max} = hf - \phi$.

As the photoelectron moves away from the sheet through the electric field, the field exerts a force on it opposite to its motion and does negative work on it ($W = qEd$), converting its kinetic energy into electrical potential energy. The electron slows down and comes to rest when the work done against the field equals its initial kinetic energy, $qEd = hf - \phi$, then is accelerated back towards the sheet. The maximum distance $d$ it travels depends on its initial kinetic energy (and so on the frequency of the light) and on the field strength.

questions.question:
A rope connects a mass on a horizontal surface to a pulley attached to an electric motor, as shown. The motor operates at voltage $V$ and draws current $I$; the coefficient of kinetic friction between the mass and the surface is $\mu_k$ and the normal force on the mass is $F_N$. Assume all the electrical power is used to pull the mass.

Assuming the mass is moving at a constant velocity, show that the velocity of the mass as it moves along the horizontal surface is given by $v = \dfrac{VI}{\mu_k F_N}$.
questions.answer:
Electrical power input to the motor: $P = VI$.

Mechanical power delivered to the mass by the rope tension $F$: $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{Fs}{t} = Fv$.

At constant velocity the net force on the mass is zero, so the tension equals the kinetic friction: $F = F_{\text{friction}} = \mu_k F_N$.

Equating the powers: $VI = \mu_k F_N v \Rightarrow v = \dfrac{VI}{\mu_k F_N}$.

questions.question:
The two graphs below show the gravitational and electrostatic forces acting between two protons in the nucleus of an atom, as a function of nucleon separation $d$.

Analyse the graphs and account for the stability of the nucleus.
questions.answer:
The gravitational force between the protons is attractive (shown as negative) but extremely weak: at $d = 1\times10^{-15}$ m it is only about $2\times10^{-34}$ N. The electrostatic (Coulomb) force is repulsive and enormously larger — about 230–250 N at the same separation — and both forces increase rapidly as $d$ decreases (inverse-square).

So gravity cannot hold the protons together against their electrostatic repulsion (it is about $10^{36}$ times weaker). The nucleus is stable because of a third force, the strong nuclear force, which acts between all nucleons (protons and neutrons), is attractive and much stronger than the electrostatic repulsion at separations of about $10^{-15}$ m, but has a very short range. Neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding electrostatic repulsion, helping bind the nucleus.

questions.question:
Below is a diagram showing the harmonics of standing waves for a string with 2 fixed ends.

Explain how the concept of standing wave harmonics can be used to improve Bohr's model of the atom.
questions.answer:
Bohr simply postulated that electrons occupy stable orbits with quantised angular momentum and do not radiate, without explaining why. De Broglie proposed that electrons have a wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$. Just as a string with fixed ends can only support standing waves with a whole number of half-wavelengths (the harmonics), an electron orbit is only stable if the electron's wave forms a standing wave around it — the circumference must be a whole number of electron wavelengths: $2\pi r = n\lambda = \dfrac{nh}{mv}$.

This gives $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, exactly Bohr's quantisation condition, so it explains why only certain orbits (and hence discrete energy levels) are allowed. Because a standing wave does not propagate, it does not transfer energy, which explains why electrons in these orbits do not continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus.

questions.question:
Unpolarised light of intensity 128 W m$^{-2}$ passes through three polarising filters. The polarising axes of the first and third filters are at $0^\circ$, and the axis of polarising material 2 is rotated by an angle $\theta$.

If the intensity of the light passing out of the third filter is 16 W m$^{-2}$, calculate the angle by which polarising material 2 is rotated.
questions.answer:
The first filter halves the intensity of unpolarised light: $I_1 = 0.5\times128 = 64.0\ \text{W m}^{-2}$.

Using Malus' law $I = I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$:

Filter 2 (at $\theta$ to filter 1): $I_2 = 64.0\cos^2\theta$

Filter 3 (also at $\theta$ to filter 2): $I_3 = I_2\cos^2\theta = 64.0\cos^4\theta$

$16 = 64.0\cos^4\theta \Rightarrow \cos^4\theta = \tfrac14 \Rightarrow \cos^2\theta = \tfrac12 \Rightarrow \theta = 45^\circ$

(Check: $I_2 = 64\times0.5 = 32$, $I_3 = 32\times0.5 = 16\ \text{W m}^{-2}$.)

questions.question: Explain why the total energy of a satellite orbiting the Earth is always negative.
questions.answer:
The total energy of an orbiting satellite is the sum of its kinetic energy and its gravitational potential energy. Gravitational potential energy is defined as zero at an infinite distance from Earth; because gravity is attractive, work must be done to move the satellite out to infinity, so at any finite distance its potential energy is negative: $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. For a circular orbit $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, which is only half the magnitude of $U$, so $E = K + U = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r} < 0$.

The negative total energy means the satellite is in a bound system: it does not have enough energy to escape Earth's gravitational field, so it remains in orbit. Energy would have to be supplied to raise its total energy to zero for it to escape.

questions.question:
In a version of Millikan's oil-drop experiment, a charged oil droplet with mass $3.6 \times 10^{-14}$ kg falls with an acceleration of 1.256 m s$^{-2}$ while the electric field is turned on. The potential difference across the electric field is $6.0 \times 10^{4}$ V and the distance of plate separation is 25 cm. Assume drag force is negligible.

Calculate the number of electrons within the charged oil droplet.
questions.answer:
Net force: $F_{\text{net}} = ma = 3.6\times10^{-14}\times1.256 = 4.522\times10^{-14}$ N (downwards)

Weight: $F_W = mg = 3.6\times10^{-14}\times9.8 = 3.528\times10^{-13}$ N

The electric force acts upwards: $F_E = F_W - F_{\text{net}} = 3.528\times10^{-13} - 4.522\times10^{-14} = 3.076\times10^{-13}$ N

Field: $E = \dfrac{V}{d} = \dfrac{6.0\times10^{4}}{0.25} = 2.4\times10^{5}\ \text{V m}^{-1}$

Charge: $q = \dfrac{F_E}{E} = \dfrac{3.076\times10^{-13}}{2.4\times10^{5}} = 1.282\times10^{-18}$ C

Number of electrons: $n = \dfrac{1.282\times10^{-18}}{1.602\times10^{-19}} = 8$ electrons

questions.question:
Consider the following statement:

> “Einstein's equation $E = mc^2$ has revolutionised science leading to significant advancements in both theoretical physics and practical applications in society.”

Justify this statement.
questions.answer:
$E = mc^2$ states that mass and energy are equivalent: a small mass corresponds to an enormous energy because $c^2 = 9\times10^{16}\ \text{m}^2\,\text{s}^{-2}$. This has transformed both theory and technology.

**Theoretical physics**
- *Stellar processes:* it explains how stars shine. In fusion (e.g. the proton–proton chain, $4\,{}^1\text{H}\rightarrow{}^4\text{He}$) the products have less mass than the reactants, and this mass defect is released as energy ($\approx 26$ MeV per helium nucleus), explaining stellar luminosities and lifetimes and the nucleosynthesis of elements.
- *Nuclear physics:* binding energy and mass defect explain nuclear stability and why both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy.
- *Big Bang and particle physics:* it underpins the conversion of radiation into matter in the early universe (pair production) and matter–antimatter annihilation, and it is a cornerstone of special relativity, changing our understanding of space, time, mass and energy.

**Practical applications**
- *Nuclear power:* controlled fission chain reactions in reactors convert mass to energy to generate electricity on a large scale with no carbon emissions.
- *Nuclear weapons:* uncontrolled fission (and fusion) chain reactions release vast energy — a major (and destructive) impact on society.
- *Particle accelerators and medicine:* accelerators convert kinetic energy into new particles of mass $m = E/c^2$, allowing the Standard Model to be tested; PET scanners detect the gamma rays produced when positrons and electrons annihilate.

Because the equation led both to major new theoretical understanding (stars, nuclei, the early universe, relativity) and to technologies that have changed society (nuclear power, weapons, accelerators, medical imaging), the statement is justified.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding how blackbody radiation changes as the temperature of the radiating object increases?
options: Both the maximum intensity and the peak wavelength increase.
The maximum intensity increases and the peak wavelength decreases.
Both the maximum intensity and the peak wavelength decrease.
The maximum intensity decreases, and the peak wavelength increases.
questions.answer: A hotter blackbody emits more energy at every wavelength, so the peak intensity increases, and by Wien's law $\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{b}{T}$ the peak wavelength decreases.

questions.question: Which particle is responsible for the force that holds quarks together?
questions.answer: The strong force between quarks is carried by gluons. (The original paper asked "Which meson…", but a gluon is a gauge boson, not a meson; the question has been reworded.)

questions.question:
An 18.5 cm diameter wire loop is initially oriented perpendicular to a 1.5 T magnetic field. In 0.20 s, the loop is rotated so its plane is parallel to the field direction.

What is the average induced emf in the loop?
questions.answer: $A = \pi (0.0925)^2 = 2.69 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}^2$. The flux falls from $BA = 1.5 \times 2.69 \times 10^{-2} = 4.03 \times 10^{-2}$ Wb to 0, so $\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{4.03 \times 10^{-2}}{0.20} = 0.20$ V.

questions.question: For a charged particle in an electric field, which of the following statements is NOT true for work done on the charge?
options: The work done on a charged particle is directly proportional to the strength of the electric field.
The work done on the charged particle is calculated using the magnitude of the displacement from the starting point.
The work done on the charged particle is dependent on the potential difference between the plates producing the electric field.
Doubling the charge of the particle has no impact on the work done on the charged particle.
questions.answer: $W = qEd = qV$, so the work done is proportional to the charge: doubling $q$ doubles the work. Statement D is false.

questions.question: A wheel with a diameter of 0.66 m experiences a tangential force of 5.30 N on its rim. Calculate the torque the wheel experiences.

A projectile launched on Earth follows the trajectory labelled X, as shown.

Another projectile is launched with identical speed and angle but on the surface of a planet where the gravitational acceleration is less than $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

Which trajectory would this other projectile follow? Air resistance can be ignored.
questions.answer: With the same launch velocity, $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ and $R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$ both increase when $g$ is smaller, and the launch angle is unchanged. D is the only path that is both higher and longer than X with the same initial direction.

questions.question:
Three parallel current-carrying wires, X, Y and Z, are shown. X carries 1.0 A, Y carries 2.0 A and Z carries 3.0 A. Y is 5 mm below X and Z is 5 mm below Y. The current in wire Y is flowing in the opposite direction to the currents in wires X and Z.

What is the net force per unit length acting on wire X?
questions.answer:
From Y (opposite currents, repel, so X is pushed up): $\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I_1 I_2}{r} = 2\times10^{-7} \times \dfrac{1.0 \times 2.0}{0.005} = 8 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ up.

From Z (same direction, attract, so X is pulled down): $2\times10^{-7} \times \dfrac{1.0 \times 3.0}{0.010} = 6 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ down.

Net: $2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ up.

questions.question: What was the significance of previous discoveries about the hydrogen spectrum to Bohr in developing his model of the atom?
options: Previous work had provided the energy values associated with electron transfers.
It provided stimulus and direction for Bohr's developing ideas.
Previous experiments were used to explain the wavelength of the spectral lines.
Bohr knew that orbiting electrons did not emit electromagnetic radiation.
questions.answer: The measured hydrogen lines (Balmer's empirical formula) gave Bohr a pattern his model had to explain, guiding his idea of quantised energy levels. The earlier work did not supply energy levels or explain the wavelengths — that was Bohr's contribution — and classical physics predicted orbiting electrons *would* radiate.

questions.question: One observation that supports Einstein's explanation of the photoelectric effect is that:
options: different cathode metals have the same threshold frequency.
less intense light requires a higher frequency for a photocurrent to be observed.
higher frequency light gives a greater work function for a particular metal.
when conditions produce photocurrent, it is detected immediately.
questions.answer: In the photon model, a single photon with $hf > \phi$ gives its energy to one electron at once, so emission is immediate even at low intensity. The wave model predicted a time delay while energy accumulated. (Threshold frequency and work function depend only on the metal.)

questions.question: A 30 V, 2.5 A AC supply is connected to an ideal transformer with 75 turns on the input side and 15 turns on the output side. What is the output voltage and current?
questions.answer:
$V_s = V_p \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = 30 \times \dfrac{15}{75} = 6$ V and $I_s = \dfrac{V_p I_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{30 \times 2.5}{6} = 12.5$ A.

Note: the original paper described a "DC current" through a "step-up" transformer. A steady DC supply induces no output voltage, and with 75 → 15 turns this is a step-down transformer, so the question has been corrected to an AC supply; the keyed answer (A) is unchanged.

questions.question:
Unpolarised light is incident from the left on three polarisers, as shown below. The transmission axes are: Case 1 — horizontal, vertical, diagonal; Case 2 — horizontal, diagonal, vertical; Case 3 — diagonal, horizontal, vertical.

In which of the following cases will some light get through?
questions.answer: Light is completely blocked whenever it meets a polariser at 90° to the previous one. In Case 1 (horizontal then vertical) and Case 3 (horizontal then vertical) a crossed pair blocks all the light. In Case 2 each successive polariser is only at 45° to the one before, so by Malus' law some light ($\tfrac{1}{2}\cos^2 45^\circ \cos^2 45^\circ = \tfrac18$ of the original intensity) gets through.

questions.question:
Kepler's Law of Periods, summarised in the equation $T^2 = kR^3$, shows a relationship between the orbital period and the radius of a planet orbiting a star.

In which of the following situations would a change in the value of the constant $k$ be needed?
options: For a planet of greater orbital period
For a planet of a smaller orbital radius
For an identical planet orbiting a different star
For a planet of different mass orbiting the same star
questions.answer: $k = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}$ depends only on the mass $M$ of the central star, so it changes only if the star changes.

questions.question:
The diagram shows a proton being fired upwards with a velocity of 1200 m/s into a uniform magnetic field of 3.00 T directed out of the page.

What is the acceleration of the proton as it enters the field?
questions.answer: $a = \dfrac{qvB}{m} = \dfrac{1.602 \times 10^{-19} \times 1200 \times 3.00}{1.673 \times 10^{-27}} = 3.45 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. By the right-hand rule (positive charge moving up, field out of the page) the force is to the right.

questions.question:
The apparatus shown in the diagram is used in an experiment to demonstrate Lenz's law. Coil J is connected in series with a variable resistor R, a battery and switch S; coil K is connected to a resistor xy.

In the experiment, the following sequence of changes is made to the apparatus:

1. Switch S is opened after having been closed for a short period of time.
2. Switch S is closed, and coil K is brought closer to coil J.
3. The resistance of R is decreased while switch S remains closed.

Which row of the table identifies the direction of the current in resistor xy after each change?

| | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | x to y | x to y | x to y |
| B | x to y | y to x | y to x |
| C | y to x | y to x | y to x |
| D | y to x | x to y | y to x |
questions.answer: Opening S makes the flux from J through K *decrease*; moving K closer and decreasing R (which increases the current in J) both make the flux through K *increase*. By Lenz's law the induced current in change 1 is opposite to that in changes 2 and 3, which are the same as each other. Only row B has this pattern (x to y, then y to x, y to x).

questions.question:
A football is kicked from ground level over horizontal ground with a speed of 25.0 m/s at an angle of 30° towards a goal. The ball travels a horizontal distance of 12.0 m before crossing the goal line.

At what height does the ball cross the goal line?

LEOSAR is a search and rescue satellite currently in a low Earth orbit of 850 km altitude and must be brought down to a lower orbit of 650 km altitude for a mission over the Pacific Ocean.

In order to be stable in the lower orbit, the speed of the LEOSAR satellite would need to
questions.answer:
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$ with $r = R_E + h$:

$v_{850} = \sqrt{\dfrac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times 6.0\times10^{24}}{7.221\times10^{6}}} = 7444.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $\quad v_{650} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4.002\times10^{14}}{7.021\times10^{6}}} = 7549.9\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

$\Delta v = 105\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, an increase (lower orbits are faster). Options C and D come from forgetting to add Earth's radius.

questions.question: How long does it take to emit one million photons from a 10 mW laser with a frequency of $4.5 \times 10^{14}$ Hz?
questions.answer: $E = hf = 6.626\times10^{-34} \times 4.5\times10^{14} = 2.98\times10^{-19}$ J per photon, so $10^6$ photons carry $2.98\times10^{-13}$ J. $t = \dfrac{E}{P} = \dfrac{2.98\times10^{-13}}{0.010} = 3.0\times10^{-11}$ s.

questions.question:
A physicist team is researching two planets, Ursae Majoris B and Ursae Majoris C, that orbit a distant star. The table shows some of the data that the team has gathered.

| Planet | Radius of orbit (m) | Orbital period (s) |
|---|---|---|
| Ursae Majoris B | $6.2 \times 10^{8}$ | $4.2 \times 10^{4}$ |
| Ursae Majoris C | $1.56 \times 10^{9}$ | $1.68 \times 10^{5}$ |

Based on the data in the table, which of the following statements is correct?
options: The acceleration due to gravity experienced by Ursae Majoris B is 2.5 times greater than that experienced by Ursae Majoris C.
The acceleration due to gravity experienced by Ursae Majoris C is 2.5 times greater than that experienced by Ursae Majoris B.
The acceleration due to gravity experienced by Ursae Majoris B is 6.3 times greater than that experienced by Ursae Majoris C.
The acceleration due to gravity experienced by Ursae Majoris C is 6.3 times greater than that experienced by Ursae Majoris B.
questions.answer: $a = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}$: $a_B = \dfrac{4\pi^2 (6.2\times10^8)}{(4.2\times10^4)^2} = 13.9\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, $a_C = \dfrac{4\pi^2(1.56\times10^9)}{(1.68\times10^5)^2} = 2.18\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, ratio $\approx 6.3$. (Equivalently $g \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$: $\left(\dfrac{1.56\times10^9}{6.2\times10^8}\right)^2 = 6.3$.)

questions.question:
Laser light of unknown wavelength was passed through a pair of slits separated by $3.00 \times 10^{-4}$ m. This produced an interference pattern on a screen 2.50 m from the slits.

The distance between the central bright spot in the interference pattern and the second bright spot above it is $9.50 \times 10^{-3}$ m, as shown in the diagram below.

The laser wavelength is closest to:
questions.answer: The marked spot is the second-order maximum ($m = 2$). For small angles $\sin\theta \approx \dfrac{y}{L}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{dy}{mL} = \dfrac{3.00\times10^{-4} \times 9.50\times10^{-3}}{2 \times 2.50} = 5.70\times10^{-7}$ m. (Taking $m = 1$ gives the distractor B.)

questions.question:
An electron enters a uniform electric field created by a pair of parallel plates. The plates are 40.0 cm apart and have a potential difference of 6.00 V between them, as shown in the diagram below.

The electron enters the electric field at $5.00 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in a direction parallel to the plates. Assuming the electron enters the field exactly halfway between the plates, what is its speed when it collides with one of the plates?
questions.answer: Moving halfway across, the electron falls through 3.00 V: $W = qV = 1.602\times10^{-19}\times 3.00 = 4.81\times10^{-19}$ J. Initial $K = \tfrac12 (9.109\times10^{-31})(5.00\times10^5)^2 = 1.14\times10^{-19}$ J. Final $K = 5.94\times10^{-19}$ J, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times5.94\times10^{-19}}{9.109\times10^{-31}}} = 1.14\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question:
A visitor at a lookout point at the top of a cliff accidentally rolls a ball off the lookout point, as shown in the diagram. It takes 3.5 seconds for the ball to land in the sea below.

Calculate the vertical distance that the ball travels before it lands in the sea.

A passenger in a sightseeing helicopter drops their phone while trying to take a photo of the scenery. When the phone is dropped, the helicopter is 200 m above the ground and travelling at a horizontal speed of $50.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Calculate the horizontal distance that the phone travels before it lands on the ground.
questions.answer:
The phone leaves with the helicopter's velocity: $u_x = 50.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $u_y = 0$.

Time of flight: $s_y = u_y t + \tfrac12 a_y t^2 \Rightarrow 200 = \tfrac12 (9.8) t^2 \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{40.8} = 6.39$ s.

Horizontal distance (no horizontal acceleration): $s_x = u_x t = 50.0 \times 6.39 = 319$ m $\approx 3.19\times10^{2}$ m.

questions.question: The Balmer series is observed when electrons in hydrogen transition to the second atomic shell ($n = 2$). Determine the lowest frequency of light observed in the Balmer series.
questions.answer:
The lowest frequency corresponds to the smallest energy change, the transition $n_i = 3 \to n_f = 2$.

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^2}\right) = 1.097\times10^{7}\left(\dfrac14 - \dfrac19\right) = 1.524\times10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1} \Rightarrow \lambda = 6.56\times10^{-7}$ m

$f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.00\times10^{8}}{6.56\times10^{-7}} = 4.57\times10^{14}$ Hz.

questions.question:
A race car is moving at constant speed around a banked circular track that has a radius of 90.0 m and an angle of banking of $\theta$ degrees, as shown in the diagram.

Identify the forces acting on the car and state the direction of each.
questions.answer:
- **Weight** (gravitational force, $mg$): acting vertically downwards.
- **Normal (reaction) force** from the track: acting perpendicular to the banked surface, i.e. tilted from the vertical by $\theta$ towards the centre of the circle.

(If the car is not at the design speed there is also a friction force along the track surface, up or down the slope.) The horizontal component of the normal force provides the centripetal force.

questions.question: A race car is moving at constant speed around a banked circular track that has a radius of 90.0 m. If the angle of banking is 10°, find the speed necessary so that no sideways force (friction) needs to be exerted between the tyres and the track.
questions.answer:
With no friction, only the weight $mg$ and the normal force $N$ act. Vertically: $N\cos\theta = mg$. Horizontally (towards the centre): $N\sin\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

Dividing: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}$, so

$v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta} = \sqrt{90.0 \times 9.8 \times \tan 10^\circ} = 12.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question: Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the Earth as it orbits the Sun. Use $1.50 \times 10^{11}$ m as the radius of Earth's orbit.
questions.answer:
$T = 365 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60 = 3.15\times10^{7}$ s

$v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 1.50\times10^{11}}{3.15\times10^{7}} = 2.99\times10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

$a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \dfrac{(2.99\times10^{4})^2}{1.50\times10^{11}} = 5.95\times10^{-3}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ towards the Sun.

questions.question: A 1500 kg spacecraft orbits the Earth at a distance of $4.00 \times 10^{7}$ m and completes an orbit in 6.00 hours. How much does the centripetal force exerted on the spacecraft while in orbit differ from the gravitational force on it if it was on the Earth's surface?
questions.answer:
$v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 4.00\times10^{7}}{21\,600} = 1.164\times10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

$a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \dfrac{(1.164\times10^{4})^2}{4.00\times10^{7}} = 3.38\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, so $F_c = ma_c = 1500 \times 3.38 = 5.08\times10^{3}$ N.

On the surface: $F_g = mg = 1500 \times 9.8 = 1.47\times10^{4}$ N.

Difference: $1.47\times10^{4} - 5.08\times10^{3} \approx 9.6\times10^{3}$ N (the centripetal force in orbit is about 9.6 kN smaller).

*Note: the paper's solution subtracts $14\,715 - 5077$ and writes 9510 N; the correct difference is about $9.6\times10^{3}$ N.*

questions.question: Referring to Kepler's laws, describe how Earth's centripetal acceleration varies as its orbit takes it closer to the Sun and further away each year.
questions.answer:
Kepler's first law states that planetary orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus, so the Earth–Sun distance $r$ varies over the year. Kepler's second law states that the line joining the planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so the Earth moves faster when it is closer to the Sun (perihelion) and slower when it is further away (aphelion).

Since $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$ (equivalently $a = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$), when Earth is closer to the Sun $v$ is larger and $r$ is smaller, so its centripetal acceleration is greatest; when it is furthest away $v$ is smaller and $r$ larger, so its centripetal acceleration is least.

*Note: the paper's sample answer attributes the equal-areas law to Kepler's third law; it is the second law (the third law relates $T^2$ to $r^3$).*

questions.question:
A particle in an accelerator reaches a velocity of $2.50 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ before entering a Wilson cloud chamber. The cloud chamber is in a uniform magnetic field of $1.95 \times 10^{-6}$ T directed into the page. The diagram illustrates the particle's path: it enters moving up the page and curves to the right.

Identify whether the particle is positively or negatively charged and justify your response.
questions.answer: The particle is **negatively charged**. For a positive charge moving up the page in a field into the page, the right-hand rule ($\vec F = q\vec v \times \vec B$) gives a force to the left. The particle curves to the right, so the force on it is opposite to that for a positive charge, and the charge must be negative.

questions.question:
A charged particle moving at $2.50 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field of $1.95 \times 10^{-6}$ T perpendicular to its velocity. The radius of the particle's circular path is 5.0 cm.

Show that the charge-to-mass ratio of the particle is $2.6 \times 10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = qvB \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$

$\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{v}{rB} = \dfrac{2.50\times10^{4}}{0.050 \times 1.95\times10^{-6}} = 2.6\times10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$

questions.question: Determine the wavelength of an electron moving at $2.0 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
questions.answer: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{9.109\times10^{-31} \times 2.0\times10^{7}} = 3.6\times10^{-11}$ m

questions.question: How was an observation from electron scattering experiments used to support de Broglie's proposal of matter waves?
questions.answer:
Davisson and Germer fired a beam of electrons at a nickel crystal and measured the intensity of the scattered electrons at different angles. They observed a diffraction pattern — strong maxima at particular angles — similar to the pattern produced when X-rays are diffracted by a crystal lattice.

Diffraction is a wave phenomenon, so this showed that electrons behave as waves. The wavelength calculated from the diffraction maxima and the crystal spacing agreed with de Broglie's predicted wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$ for the electrons' momentum, providing experimental confirmation of matter waves.

questions.question: Explain why matter waves have not been observed for objects larger than single molecules.
questions.answer: The de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$ is inversely proportional to mass. Because $h$ is so small ($6.626\times10^{-34}$ J s), any macroscopic object has a wavelength many orders of magnitude smaller than an atom. Diffraction and interference are only observable when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the gap or obstacle, and no slit or grating that small exists, so wave behaviour cannot be detected.

questions.question: How far above the Earth's surface will an object need to ascend for the acceleration due to gravity to be half what it is at the surface? (Radius of Earth $= 6.38\times10^{6}$ m.)
questions.answer:
$g = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$. For $g = \tfrac12 g_{\text{surface}}$: $\dfrac{GM}{r^2} = \dfrac12 \dfrac{GM}{R_E^2} \Rightarrow r^2 = 2R_E^2 \Rightarrow r = \sqrt2\,R_E$.

Height above the surface: $h = r - R_E = (\sqrt2 - 1)R_E = 0.414 \times 6.38\times10^{6} = 2.64\times10^{6}$ m.

questions.question: How long would a day be if the Earth were rotating so fast that objects at the equator were apparently weightless? (Radius of Earth $= 6.38\times10^{6}$ m.)
questions.answer:
Objects are apparently weightless when gravity provides exactly the centripetal acceleration needed: $g = \dfrac{v^2}{R_E} = \dfrac{4\pi^2 R_E}{T^2}$.

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R_E}{g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{6.38\times10^{6}}{9.80}} = 5.07\times10^{3}$ s $\approx 84.5$ minutes (about 1.4 hours).

questions.question:
A Physics student is provided with two pairs of polarised sunglasses and a light source of polarised light. The two sunglasses are oriented at 42.0° to one another. The light source is polarised at a 21.0° angle to the first pair of sunglasses.

What percentage of the incoming intensity is transmitted once it has passed through both sunglasses?
questions.answer:
By Malus' law $I = I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$. The angle between the light and the first polariser is 21.0°, and between the two polarisers 42.0°:

$I_2 = I_0 \cos^2 21.0^\circ \cos^2 42.0^\circ = I_0 (0.8716)(0.5523) = 0.481\,I_0$

So 48.1% of the incoming intensity is transmitted.

*Note: the paper's working writes $\cos 21.0^\circ$ and $\cos 42.0^\circ$ without the squares, although its final answer (48.1%) is the Malus' law value.*

questions.question: Discuss how polarisation can be explained by comparing the particle model and wave models of light.
questions.answer:
Polarisation is the restriction of the oscillations of a wave to a single plane. If light passes through one polariser and then through a second polariser whose axis is perpendicular to the first, no light passes through the second, and the transmitted intensity varies with the angle between them ($I = I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$).

**Particle model.** Newton's corpuscular model describes light as a stream of particles. Such particles have no orientation that a polariser could select, so they would be expected to pass through both polarisers regardless of angle; the model cannot explain polarisation.

**Longitudinal wave model.** Huygens' wave model treated light as a longitudinal wave (like sound). In a longitudinal wave the oscillation is parallel to the direction of propagation, so there is no transverse direction to restrict — longitudinal waves cannot be polarised. This model also fails.

**Transverse (electromagnetic) wave model.** Maxwell showed light is an electromagnetic wave: oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. Because the oscillations are transverse, a polariser can transmit only the component of the electric field along its axis, explaining both the complete blocking by crossed polarisers and Malus' law. Polarisation therefore supports the transverse wave model of light.

questions.question: AC induction motors and electromagnetic braking have features in common. With reference to relevant physics concepts, explain these by outlining the operation of both.
questions.answer:
**Common features.** Both rely on electromagnetic induction (Faraday's law, $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$) and Lenz's law: a changing magnetic flux through a conductor induces currents whose own magnetic field opposes the change, producing a force on the conductor. In both, there is no physical/electrical contact between the source of the field and the moving conductor, reducing wear and maintenance.

**AC induction motor.** The stator has sets of coils (e.g. three-phase, 120° out of phase) arranged around the rotor; the AC supply makes the resultant magnetic field rotate. The rotor is a "squirrel cage" of conducting bars joined by end rings. The rotating field changes the flux through the cage, inducing emf and currents in the bars (Faraday). The induced currents experience a force in the magnetic field (motor effect), and by Lenz's law the rotor turns in the direction that reduces the relative motion between it and the rotating field — so it follows the field, always slightly slower (slip).

**Electromagnetic braking.** When a conductor (a metal rail, fin or disc, e.g. on a train or amusement-park ride) moves relative to a strong magnetic field, the flux through regions of the conductor changes, inducing eddy currents. By Lenz's law these eddy currents produce magnetic fields that oppose the relative motion, giving a retarding force that converts kinetic energy to heat in the conductor. The braking force is larger at higher speeds and fades as the object slows.

questions.question:
A physicist conducted an experiment using a transformer. The results are recorded in the table.

| | Primary coil | Secondary coil |
|---|---|---|
| Voltage (V) | 120 | ? |
| Current (mA) | 3.0 | 30 |
| Number of turns | ? | 5 |

If the transformer is 100% efficient, determine the secondary voltage and the number of turns in the primary coil.
questions.answer:
$V_p I_p = V_s I_s \Rightarrow V_s = \dfrac{V_p I_p}{I_s} = \dfrac{120 \times 3.0}{30} = 12$ V

$\dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s} \Rightarrow N_p = \dfrac{V_p N_s}{V_s} = \dfrac{120 \times 5}{12} = 50$ turns

questions.question:
A 95 W transformer is installed and has an output voltage of 12 V and an input current of 25 A.

Determine if the transformer is a step-up or step-down transformer and by what factor the voltage is multiplied.
questions.answer:
Assuming 100% efficiency, the input voltage is $V_p = \dfrac{P}{I_p} = \dfrac{95}{25} = 3.8$ V.

Since $V_p < V_s$ (3.8 V in, 12 V out), it is a **step-up** transformer.

Factor: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{12}{3.8} = 3.2$

questions.question: Using relevant equations and diagrams, describe how the motor effect plays a part in the operation of a simple DC electric motor.
questions.answer:
The motor effect is the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, $F = lIB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the current and the field; its direction is given by the right-hand rule.

In a simple DC motor a rectangular coil ABCD sits between the poles of a magnet and can rotate about an axis. Current flows in opposite directions along the two sides that are perpendicular to the field (AB and CD), so the motor-effect forces on these sides are equal and opposite (e.g. down on AB, up on CD). Being on opposite sides of the axis, they form a couple producing a torque

$$\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$$

(or $\tau = r_\perp F$), which turns the coil. (A diagram would show the coil between N and S poles with the field from N to S, the current around the loop, and force arrows up on one side and down on the other.)

The torque is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field and zero when it is perpendicular. After each half-turn the sides swap positions, so the current must be reversed to keep the torque in the same direction; the split-ring commutator does this, with brushes maintaining contact with the supply, so the coil rotates continuously in one direction.

questions.question: Discuss how interference patterns were used to provide evidence for the nature of both light and matter.
questions.answer:
**Light.** Newton proposed a particle (corpuscular) model of light, while Huygens proposed a wave model. Young's double-slit experiment produced an interference pattern of alternating bright and dark fringes. Particles would produce only two bright bands; the fringes can only be explained by waves from the two slits superposing constructively and destructively. This supported Huygens' wave model and led to the rejection of Newton's particle model (until the photon model was later needed for the photoelectric effect).

**Matter.** Electrons were thought to be purely particles. De Broglie proposed that matter has a wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$. Davisson and Germer scattered electrons off a nickel crystal and observed a diffraction/interference pattern, and the wavelength calculated from the pattern matched de Broglie's prediction. This showed electrons have wave properties.

**Overall.** Interference — a uniquely wave phenomenon — was the key evidence that changed both models, leading to the acceptance that light and matter each have a dual wave–particle nature, the basis of quantum mechanics.

questions.question:
Diagram 1 shows a small section of the spectrum for a mixture of gaseous elements (bright lines at 565, 569, 575, 582, 587, 594 and 600 nm). Diagram 2 shows the electron energy levels for a gaseous element X.

A physics student states that the spectral line produced when an electron falls from the $-3.54$ eV energy level to the $-5.74$ eV level proves that element X is one of the gases in the mixture.

Critically evaluate the student's statement using your understanding of how spectral lines are produced.
questions.answer:
Spectral lines are produced when an electron in an excited atom falls from a higher energy level to a lower one, emitting a photon whose energy equals the difference between the levels, $\Delta E = hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$. Each element has its own set of energy levels and so its own characteristic set of lines.

For the transition shown: $\Delta E = -3.54 - (-5.74) = 2.20$ eV $= 2.20 \times 1.602\times10^{-19} = 3.52\times10^{-19}$ J

$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{3.52\times10^{-19}} = 5.64\times10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 564$ nm

This is very close to the 565 nm line (the far-left line) in Diagram 1, which is evidence *consistent with* element X being in the mixture.

However, the statement that this *proves* X is present is not justified. A single matching line is not enough: different elements can have lines at the same or very similar wavelengths, and the 1 nm difference is within experimental uncertainty but is not an exact match. An element is identified by its complete pattern of lines, so further evidence is needed — for example, calculating the wavelengths of other transitions of element X (e.g. from the −1.45 / −1.47 eV levels) and showing that they also appear in the spectrum. Scientific evidence can support a conclusion but does not "prove" it from one observation.

Judgement: the data support the possibility that X is present, but the student's claim of proof is overstated.

questions.question:
A team of physicists conducted an experiment to investigate the photoelectric effect. They directed light of different frequencies at the surface of a particular metal. The maximum kinetic energies of the electrons emitted by the metal were measured, and the data was recorded in the table.

| Light frequency ($\times 10^{14}$ Hz) | Maximum kinetic energy of electrons (eV) |
|---|---|
| 5.6 | 0.01 |
| 6.0 | 0.18 |
| 6.5 | 0.41 |
| 7.1 | 0.70 |
| 7.9 | 0.97 |
| 8.8 | 1.31 |

Plot the data on a graph of maximum kinetic energy (eV) against frequency, draw a line of best fit, and, using the plotted data:

- determine the work function ($\phi$) of the metal;
- calculate a value for Planck's constant.
questions.answer:
Plot $K_{\max}$ (vertical axis, eV) against $f$ (horizontal axis, $\times10^{14}$ Hz), draw the line of best fit through the points and extend it back to the vertical axis. Since $K_{\max} = hf - \phi$, the gradient is $h$ and the vertical intercept is $-\phi$.

Extrapolating, the line meets the vertical axis at about $-2.13$ eV, so $\phi \approx 2.13$ eV (accept 2.10–2.30 eV).

Gradient, e.g. from $(1.0\times10^{14}, -1.75)$ to $(5.5\times10^{14}, 0)$: $h = \dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \dfrac{0 - (-1.75)}{5.5\times10^{14} - 1.0\times10^{14}} = \dfrac{1.75}{4.5\times10^{14}} = 3.9\times10^{-15}$ eV s (accept $3.5$–$4.5\times10^{-15}$ eV s; the accepted value is $4.14\times10^{-15}$ eV s).

questions.question:
In a photoelectric effect experiment on a particular metal, a graph of the data gave a work function of $\phi = 2.13$ eV and a value for Planck's constant of $h = 3.9 \times 10^{-15}$ eV s.

Light of wavelength 420 nm is directed at the metal. Using these values for $\phi$ and $h$, determine whether the photoelectric effect will occur.
questions.answer:
$K_{\max} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi = \dfrac{3.9\times10^{-15} \times 3.00\times10^{8}}{4.20\times10^{-7}} - 2.13 = 2.79 - 2.13 = 0.66$ eV

Since the photon energy (2.79 eV) exceeds the work function, $K_{\max} > 0$: electrons are emitted with up to 0.66 eV of kinetic energy, so the photoelectric effect **will occur**.

questions.question: What is the name of the following device (a coil turned by a handle between the poles of a magnet, connected to the external circuit through slip rings and carbon brushes)?
questions.answer: The coil is turned mechanically (by the handle) in a magnetic field, so an emf is induced: it is a generator. Each end of the coil is connected to its own **slip ring**, so the connection to the external circuit is never reversed and the output alternates direction every half turn — an AC generator. (A DC generator would use a split-ring commutator.)

questions.question: An object is moving in a horizontal circle on a string with a constant angular velocity $\omega$. The tension in the string, which is approximately horizontal, is $F$. If $\omega$ is doubled while all the other quantities are kept constant, what will the tension in the string become?
questions.answer: The tension provides the centripetal force: $F = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$ (since $v = \omega r$). With $m$ and $r$ fixed, $F \propto \omega^2$, so doubling $\omega$ gives $2^2 F = 4F$.

questions.question: If an astronaut orbiting the Earth near its surface were to stand on a set of bathroom scales, why would there be a reading of zero?
options: The strength of the gravitational field is zero.
The pull of the Earth is balanced by the pull of the Moon.
The astronaut falls towards the Earth at the same rate as the space capsule.
questions.answer: Near the Earth's surface $g$ is still about $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, and mass does not change. The astronaut, scales and capsule are all in free fall with the same centripetal acceleration $g$, so there is no normal force between the astronaut and the scales — apparent weightlessness.

questions.question:
An object is executing uniform circular motion anticlockwise, as shown in the figure. P is the left-most point of the circle.

At position P, which of the following shows the directions of the instantaneous velocity $\vec{v}$ and acceleration $\vec{a}$?
questions.answer: Moving anticlockwise, at the left-most point the object is moving straight down, tangent to the circle. In uniform circular motion the acceleration is centripetal, pointing towards the centre, which from P is to the right.

questions.question:
Iodine-131 is a radioisotope used in nuclear medicine. It has a half-life of 8 hours and eventually becomes a stable isotope xenon-131 according to the equation

$$^{131}_{\ 53}\text{I} \rightarrow {}^{131}_{\ 54}\text{Xe} + \gamma$$

24.0 mg of iodine-131 is injected in the body of a patient.

How many milligrams of xenon-131, produced as a result of this reaction, are present in the body after 16 hours?
questions.answer: 16 hours is 2 half-lives, so the iodine remaining is $24.0 \times \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = 6.0$ mg. The decayed iodine has become xenon of the same mass number (mass changes negligibly), so the xenon present is $24.0 - 6.0 = 18.0$ mg.

questions.question:
A horizontal metal cylinder PQ, perpendicular to the page (end P nearest the viewer), moves down between two current-carrying solenoids, as shown below.

Which of the following correctly shows the direction of the magnetic field between the solenoids and the charge at P?
options: Magnetic field: left; charge at P: positive
Magnetic field: left; charge at P: negative
Magnetic field: right; charge at P: positive
Magnetic field: right; charge at P: negative
questions.answer:
Applying the right-hand grip rule to the currents in the windings (from the battery polarities), both solenoids produce a field directed to the **left** in the gap between them.

The free charges in the cylinder move down with it, so each experiences $\vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$. With $\vec{v}$ down and $\vec{B}$ to the left, the right-hand palm rule gives a force on positive charge **into the page**, i.e. towards end Q (electrons are pushed towards P). So Q becomes positive and P becomes **negative**.

questions.question:
A radioactive isotope decays by alpha and beta particle emission. Over a number of decays, the nucleon number decreases by 4 while the proton number is unchanged.

How many alpha and beta particles have been emitted?
questions.answer: Only alpha decay changes the nucleon number ($A$ decreases by 4 per alpha), so there was exactly **1 alpha**, which reduced $Z$ by 2. Each $\beta^-$ decay increases $Z$ by 1 with no change in $A$, so **2 beta** decays are needed to restore the proton number.

questions.question:
Two students are discussing the advantages of magnetic brakes.

Student A says that because the magnetic force is proportional to velocity they provide a smoother braking action.

Student B says that because magnetic fields do no work, the brakes produce no heat.

Which of the students, if any, is/are correct?
options: Both student A and student B
Neither student A nor student B
questions.answer: The eddy currents, and hence the opposing (Lenz's law) force, are proportional to the rate of change of flux, i.e. to the speed, so braking is strong at high speed and gentle at low speed — smooth (Student A is correct). The kinetic energy removed is converted by the eddy currents into heat in the conductor ($P = I^2R$), so Student B is wrong.

questions.question:
Control rods and moderators play a key role in controlling the rate of fission in nuclear reactors.

Which of the following correctly shows how this is achieved?
options: Control rod: by absorbing neutrons. Moderator: by slowing down fast neutrons to thermal speeds.
Control rod: by absorbing neutrons. Moderator: by speeding up slow neutrons so that a chain reaction is sustainable.
Control rod: by increasing the capture cross-section of neutrons. Moderator: by speeding up slow neutrons so that a chain reaction is sustainable.
Control rod: by increasing the capture cross-section of neutrons. Moderator: by slowing down fast neutrons to thermal speeds.
questions.answer: Control rods (e.g. boron, cadmium) absorb neutrons, reducing the number available to cause further fissions. The moderator (e.g. graphite, water) slows fast fission neutrons to thermal speeds, at which they are much more likely to be captured by U-235 and cause fission.

questions.question:
This is a Hertzsprung–Russell (H–R) diagram showing many star plots. The axes are not labelled (the conventional orientation is used).

Which of the following statements is true of the luminosity and temperature of stars A and B?
options: The luminosity of star A is lower while the temperature of star B is higher.
The luminosity of star A is lower while the temperature of star B is lower.
The luminosity of star A is higher while the temperature of star B is higher.
The luminosity of star A is higher while the temperature of star B is lower.
questions.answer: On an H–R diagram luminosity increases upwards and surface temperature increases to the **left**. Star A (on the main sequence) is higher than star B (a white dwarf), so A has the higher luminosity; B is further left, so B has the higher temperature.

questions.question: Unpolarised light passes through two polaroid sheets. At what angle $\theta$ between the transmission axes of the two sheets should they be placed to reduce the intensity by ninety percent?
questions.answer: The first polaroid halves the intensity of unpolarised light: $I_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0$. Malus' law at the second: $I_2 = I_1\cos^2\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0\cos^2\theta$. A 90% reduction means $I_2 = 0.1I_0$, so $\cos^2\theta = 0.2$ and $\theta = \cos^{-1}\sqrt{0.2}$. (Option D would only apply to light already polarised along the first sheet's axis.)

questions.question:
The diagram shows a discharge tube used by Thomson to investigate cathode rays. When the connections are made to a high voltage power supply, cathode rays are produced at C and accelerated across AB and through parallel plates P and Q, connected to a second power supply, with P (the upper plate) positively charged. The rays then hit the centre of the fluorescent screen when a magnetic field is applied (along the XY direction, perpendicular to the page) between the plates P and Q.

Which of the following shows the aim of this experiment and the correct direction of the applied magnetic field?
options: Aim: to determine the charge of the electron. Magnetic field: from X to Y.
Aim: to determine the charge of the electron. Magnetic field: from Y to X.
Aim: to determine the charge to mass ratio of the electron. Magnetic field: from X to Y.
Aim: to determine the charge to mass ratio of the electron. Magnetic field: from Y to X.
questions.answer: Thomson's crossed-field experiment measured $\dfrac{q}{m}$ of the electron (the charge itself was found by Millikan). The electric field pushes the negative cathode rays up towards P, so the magnetic force must be **down** for the rays to pass undeflected ($qE = qvB$). For a negative charge moving to the right with a downward force, the right-hand palm rule (reversed for negative charge) gives $\vec{B}$ **into the page**, i.e. from Y (front) to X (back).

questions.question: Two satellites orbit a planet. One of the satellites has an orbital radius of $2.3 \times 10^{6}$ m and a period of $7.6 \times 10^{4}$ s. The other satellite has an orbital period of $1.3 \times 10^{5}$ s. What is the orbital radius of this second satellite?
questions.answer:
By Kepler's third law $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}$ is the same for both satellites:

$$r_2 = r_1\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^{2/3} = 2.3 \times 10^{6} \times \left(\frac{1.3 \times 10^{5}}{7.6 \times 10^{4}}\right)^{2/3} = 2.3 \times 10^{6} \times 1.43 \approx 3.3 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$$

questions.question:
A 500 kg satellite is initially in a circular orbit with a radius of 10 000 km around the Earth. The satellite is then moved to a new circular orbit with a radius of 20 000 km.

What is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the satellite?
questions.answer:
$$\Delta U = -\frac{GMm}{r_2} - \left(-\frac{GMm}{r_1}\right) = GMm\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right)$$
